title: Certification Guide
summary: Four logos on four bottles can mean four different things. This is what each certification actually verifies, what it does not, and where the phrase ‘cruelty-free’ carries no legal weight at all.

schemes.name: Leaping Bunny
schemes.operator: Cruelty Free International and the Coalition for Consumer Information on Cosmetics
verifies: No animal testing by the company, its suppliers, or any third party acting on its behalf
A fixed cut-off date after which no animal testing may occur anywhere in the supply chain
Written declarations obtained from every ingredient supplier
A supplier monitoring system, re-committed to annually
Independent audits available to the certifying body
doesNotVerify: That the product is vegan — Leaping Bunny concerns testing, not ingredients
That the parent company applies the same standard across its other brands
schemes.note: The fixed cut-off date is the mechanism that distinguishes this scheme. A company cannot certify a product, then later commission testing on a reformulated ingredient and keep the mark.

schemes.name: PETA Beauty Without Bunnies
schemes.operator: People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals
verifies: A signed statement of assurance from the company covering itself and its ingredient suppliers
A commitment not to conduct or commission animal testing anywhere in the world
Two published categories: ‘Animal Test-Free’ and ‘Animal Test-Free and Vegan’
doesNotVerify: Independent audit of the declaration — the scheme is documentation-based
Supplier-level evidence beyond the company's own assurance
schemes.note: A larger database with faster listing, resting on company attestation rather than audit. That is a real difference in evidential weight, not a reason to dismiss it.

schemes.name: Vegan trademarks
schemes.operator: The Vegan Society; Vegan Action / Certified Vegan; others
verifies: No animal-derived ingredients in the formulation
In most schemes, no animal testing commissioned by the company
doesNotVerify: The supply-chain testing position with the rigour of a dedicated testing scheme
That no animal testing occurred at ingredient level historically
schemes.note: The most common point of confusion on a shelf. Vegan is a claim about what is in the bottle. Cruelty-free is a claim about how what is in the bottle was assessed. A product can be either without being both.

schemes.name: Uncertified ‘not tested on animals’ claims
verifies: Nothing that has been checked by anyone outside the company
doesNotVerify: Whether the claim covers ingredients or only the finished product
Whether it covers suppliers and contract laboratories
Whether testing occurred before an unstated cut-off date
Whether testing is commissioned in markets that require it
schemes.note: In many markets this phrasing is unregulated. The most common construction — literally true, materially incomplete — is a finished-product claim on a product whose ingredients were animal-tested by a supplier. Canada's 2023 reform is notable precisely because it made false cruelty-free claims actionable.

questions.title: Four questions that separate a claim from a commitment
items: Does the claim cover ingredients, or only the finished product?
Does it extend to suppliers and contract laboratories, or stop at the company's own facilities?
Is there a fixed cut-off date, or is the claim written in the present tense only?
Does the company sell in markets where an authority may require testing — and if so, under what exemption?
